Wholesale banks have digitized many credit tasks but still run lending decisions as a handoff-heavy sequence. BCG argues that agentic AI can turn credit assessment into a continuously updated capability—provided banks redesign processes, data, and controls rather than add another standalone tool.

The bottleneck is the operating model, not individual credit toolsAnalysts still connect data, systems, approvals, and exceptions manually, causing completed work to go stale. Redesigning this flow can reduce decision time by 40%–60%.

Always-on monitoring shifts credit officers from assembly to judgmentAgents can update only the affected elements when financials, covenants, or payment behavior change. That enables risk teams to identify 80%–90% of deteriorating credits early enough to intervene.

Banks must build a shared credit ecosystem, not isolated AI pilotsReusable capabilities—such as document reading, financial analysis, and policy validation—need common data definitions, audit trails, and governance. Wholesale credit processes remain surprisingly manual. When a company seeks financing, analysts still have to assemble much of the credit picture themselves: pulling financial statements from public filings, reconciling them with information already in the bank’s systems, updating the borrower’s risk rating and lending limits, preparing the credit memo, and tracking down missing documents and approvals. Banks have spent years digitizing individual steps, but the process itself remains largely sequential. One task waits for another, and the file often waits for a person. Better tools for analyzing financials, calculating ratings, or managing documents can make individual steps faster without eliminating those handoffs.Agentic AI creates an opportunity to change that pattern. Rather than simply helping analysts complete individual tasks faster, banks can use agents to coordinate work across systems and keep the credit file current as new information arrives. New financial statements can trigger an update to the borrower’s financial analysis; new covenant information can prompt a recalculation of whether the borrower remains within agreed thresholds; and a credit rating change or deterioration in payment behavior can automatically refresh the parts of the assessment that depend on it. By the time a client makes a request, much of the underlying credit work can already be up to date.The potential impact is significant. BCG project experience indicates that banks redesigning the process in this way can reduce time to decision by 40% to 60% compared with traditional automation, particularly for mid-market and large corporate clients. But speed is only part of the opportunity. The larger prize is to free credit professionals to focus on judgment, respond to clients faster, and give risk functions a more continuous view of the portfolio.The Constraint Is the Process, Not the Tooling
Most banks have already invested in technology tools that perform individual credit tasks well. The constraint is the operating model around them: work still moves through a series of handoffs, with people responsible for connecting systems, resolving exceptions, and determining when the next step can begin.Several sources of friction reinforce one another. The process remains fundamentally linear: a delay at one stage can hold up everything downstream, while work already completed begins to go stale. Unit cost rises with variability, as differences across industries, borrowers, and deal structures turn many files into bespoke exercises. The process is also episodic, usually triggered by a request or renewal date, which leaves monitoring between those events more reactive. And persistent data friction means teams often have to extract and reconcile information across email, spreadsheets, and core systems before risk judgment can begin. At the same time, regulatory expectations around documentation, traceability, and evidence of repayment capacity continue to increase.These constraints explain why improving individual tools produces only incremental gains. A faster rating engine or better document system can accelerate one part of the process without changing how work moves through the whole. As long as people remain the connective tissue between otherwise capable systems, much of the potential benefit remains out of reach.

From a Sequence to a Standing Capability
The shift that agents enable is not simply that each step runs faster. It is that the process no longer has to operate as a queue. In an agentic design, the system is always on and responds to signals rather than waiting for a person to start the next task. As new information arrives, the system can update only the parts of the credit file that depend on it, rather than restarting the process or moving sequentially from one stage to the next.That changes the role of the credit officer as well as the flow of work. (See Exhibit 1.) Today, people often sit inside the loop: the process waits for them to collect information, reconcile systems, move work from one stage to the next, and resolve gaps before the file can advance. In the agentic model, more of that assembly and coordination happens continuously across the system. The credit officer moves above the loop, reviewing what the system has assembled, challenging exceptions, and applying judgment where it is needed.

Agents can turn the credit process from a sequence of tasks into a standing capability that keeps the file current between formal review points. When a client request arrives, much of the underlying work has already been done. That is the logic behind the 40% to 60% reduction in time to decision observed in comparable transformations.What It Is Worth, and to Whom
The case for agentic credit is often framed in terms of cost. But for a chief risk officer (CRO), it’s often not the most important issue. Many of the gains associated with agentic credit begin with improvements to the underlying platform and data, which can increase the share of applications processed without manual intervention by 10 to 20 percentage points. From there, banks can redesign decision rules and processes and use agents to remove the handoffs and rework that remain. Together, these changes can increase automation substantially and reduce time to decision, although the potential varies by segment. (See Exhibit 2.)

Banks can capture value in three ways:Released Capacity. Where processes are redesigned rather than simply accelerated, capacity requirements in risk and operations can fall by as much as 40% to 50%, while relationship managers can recover 30% to 40% of their time for client coverage. What banks do with that capacity is a choice; in our experience, most redeploy it.Faster Client Response. In wholesale banking, speed can be commercially important. A shorter time to decision gives a bank an advantage when a client is comparing financing options or working against a transaction timetable. Value is created by having more of the underlying credit work already completed when the client needs an answer.Earlier Risk Intervention. For the CRO, a more consequential benefit may be a shift from periodic review toward continuous, event-driven monitoring. The entire portfolio can be screened continuously, allowing 80% to 90% of deteriorating credits to be identified early enough for the bank to act. Of those credits, 30% to 50% can be restructured while still in Stage 2 of the three-stage accounting framework for credit losses—when credit risk has increased but the exposure is not yet impaired—potentially limiting further deterioration and the need for additional provisions. A consolidated view of each borrower’s total exposure can also help the bank manage limits when credit is originated rather than correct excesses later at the portfolio level. And 50% to 60% of annual reviews can be closed quickly when nothing material has changed, allowing analysts to focus on the exceptions.The degree of automation will vary with the complexity of the credit. Small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) lending offers greater scope for automation because applications tend to be more standardized, while large corporate credits are more often bespoke and negotiated. But lower automation in large corporate lending does not mean lower value. Exposures are bigger, the commercial cost of a slow response can be greater, and the consequences of missing an emerging risk can be measured in credit losses and provisions rather than staff time.Build an Ecosystem, Not a Product
A common mistake is to treat agentic credit as a single application, often a tool for drafting the credit memo. In practice, the opportunity spans the life of an exposure—qualifying opportunities, assessing risk, drafting and maintaining the memo, validating it against policy, booking the credit, monitoring it, and responding when something changes.Those are separate solutions, with different owners and business cases, but many of the underlying capabilities are the same. An agent that reads a set of statutory accounts, normalizes the information, and produces the relevant ratios can support both an origination case and a later monitoring review. The same is true of external data retrieval, document processing, peer benchmarking, and narrative drafting. Reusing those capabilities across solutions is an important part of the economics: once a capability has been built, later solutions can draw on it rather than recreate it.That reuse depends on a shared foundation. (See Exhibit 3.) Guardrails, model life-cycle management, audit trails, and a common data ontology need to work across the ecosystem rather than being rebuilt for each use case. The ontology is particularly important because it allows the system to understand how a client, application, rating, contract, and covenant relate to one another.

That is also why isolated pilots can become difficult to scale. They may prove that an individual use case works, but if each solution is built independently, the bank can end up rebuilding capabilities and infrastructure it already has.Leading banks therefore design the target ecosystem broadly and then build it in waves, rather than discovering the architecture one pilot at a time. The aim is to establish the shared capabilities and foundation early enough that later solutions can build on them. One European wholesale bank has designed an ecosystem of 15 agents across credit and has begun deploying them in stages, starting with four that provide the building blocks for those that follow.The same logic applies to the business case. Because many capabilities are shared across solutions and segments, funding them agent by agent can leave the common foundation without a clear owner. A single business case for wholesale lending is often the better starting point, with separate cases only where the economics are genuinely different. That matters in a sector where more than 60% of bank technology spending typically goes toward running the bank rather than changing it.Inside a Solution: One System Writes, Another Challenges
The risk function’s confidence in a credit memo solution depends on how it is designed to maintain control. A well-designed solution can be thought of as two subsystems working from one shared record of facts. (See Exhibit 4.)

The first compiles and maintains the file. Specialized agents read the sources they are designed to handle—including filings, exchange disclosures, documents from rating agencies and sector bodies, information from the bank’s own systems, and documents uploaded by analysts—and convert what they find into individual facts. Together, that information forms a client-level knowledge base—a structured record of the borrower that includes both current information and relevant history, such as earlier reports, past credit decisions, prior memos, and exceptions. Each fact carries information about its source, the date it was read, and the person or system that produced it. Other agents can then draft sections of the memo from that client knowledge base. A number that appears in the memo without a supporting fact is treated as a defect.The second subsystem challenges and validates the output against the bank’s written rules. Arithmetic checks—whether limit grids reconcile, tenors are within permitted limits, financial statements are still current, or a leverage test falls into a defined category—can be handled mechanically. Where judgment is required, a citation-bound agent can identify the standard, evidence, and proposed correction behind each finding. A person reviews each finding before it is applied.Three design principles are especially important:Don’t let language models compute numbers. Ratios, concentration percentages, and limit totals should come from deterministic code. Agents can explain and contextualize those figures, but they should not derive them. That makes the output easier to defend to model-risk functions and supervisors.Use the bank’s existing deterministic layer. An agent doesn’t need to recreate the rating model, pricing engine, limit system, scoring model, or stress grid. It can call the tools the institution has already built, validated, and approved, using the inputs it has assembled. In that sense, the agentic layer orchestrates existing risk infrastructure rather than replacing it.Use deterministic checks wherever possible. Where the answer can be determined by code, the challenge layer should use deterministic checks. Whether a figure lacks a supporting fact or a citation resolves to nothing is not a matter of judgment. Using a language model for those checks can introduce uncertainty. Model-based judgment should be reserved for cases where judgment is unavoidable, with the credit officer retaining the final say. This is also where the “above the loop” concept becomes most concrete. The credit officer is not removed from the process; the role changes from assembling the file to reviewing, challenging, correcting, and deciding.What It Takes
Only 5% of companies are achieving AI value at scale, while 60% are not yet generating material value from their AI investments, according to a BCG study. Engineering is only part of the challenge. In BCG’s experience, roughly 10% of the effort in an AI transformation should go to algorithms, 20% to technology and data, and 70% to people and processes. For banks, that means investing not only in the models themselves but also in the harness engineering around them—the governance, controls, context, and operating structures that allow agents to work reliably at scale.Several design and operating choices are especially important.Start with a clear perimeter. Before choosing the first use cases to build, banks should define the target ecosystem. The initial scope should be manageable, with a specific client segment and set of deal types. Highly complex products such as structured finance can be left for later where appropriate. The solution can then expand progressively toward the broader target without forcing the bank to discover its architecture one pilot at a time.Define the standards and knowledge base before you build. Agents need examples of good work and a clear description of the defects they must catch. Gold-standard credit memos agreed upon by senior credit professionals, together with a set of failures that the system must identify in real files, provide the benchmarks against which the system is tested. Banks should also build a curated knowledge base for the chosen perimeter, bringing together the relevant policies, guidelines, examples, and other institutional knowledge that agents can draw on for analysis and validation. This pool of knowledge cannot be bought off the shelf because it encodes the bank’s own judgment. Testing should continue after go-live; validation and monitoring are ongoing operating requirements.Make provenance a property of the system. Every figure should carry its source with it. That allows reviewers to trace a number back to the sentence it came from, respond to supervisory questions, and distinguish information that was read from information that may have been generated.Invest in the ontology before the agents. Agents need to understand how the core objects in the credit process relate to one another; for example, that a particular contract belongs to a particular client and sits under a particular rating. Banks need to map those concepts and relationships, the data that agents will require, and the internal systems that hold the data. Doing that work up front creates a consistent data foundation for the solutions that follow.Give the solution a clear owner. Building and scaling agentic credit requires a cross-functional team, not simply an AI development team. A product owner should be accountable for the solution, supported by people who bring together AI expertise with credit-risk and business knowledge.Reduce human oversight only when warranted. Banks can reduce human oversight progressively, and only where the evidence supports doing so. This is also where the differences between segments become more pronounced: the underlying capabilities may be similar across SME and large corporate credit, but the point at which the human gate can safely be removed will differ.

The banks moving fastest in agentic credit are not necessarily those with the most advanced models. They are the ones treating agentic credit primarily as a process redesign, with AI as an enabling component and credit professionals at the center. Turning the credit file into a continuously maintained capability will take more than a successful pilot. Banks that complete the hard work of rebuilding their processes will respond to clients faster, identify deterioration earlier, and allow credit officers to spend more of their time where their judgment adds the most value. For the rest, the file will keep waiting for a person.
